title: The job above the job
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Hughes reports that on her recent NPQH cohort, almost all participants began interested in headship, and by the end of the eighteen-month course almost nobody was, a pattern she says is becoming widespread as leaders 'do the maths' on what senior leadership costs. Drawing on the Teaching Commission's July 2025 report and Craig Lomas's chapter comparing two contrasting school cultures, she distinguishes informal 'talent spotting' from real 'talent building', and cites data showing only 42% of deputy and assistant heads aspire to headship, with the average leader working 57.6 hours a week. Her sharpest argument is that when personal sacrifice becomes routine and wrapped in moral purpose, it becomes harder to challenge - 'once the exceptional becomes routine, we have stopped describing commitment and started disguising bad design'. She closes by arguing retention is about dignity as much as workload, and that middle leadership needs real time and real projects, not vague encouragement, if the leadership pipeline is to recover.
points: Hughes's observation that almost her entire NPQH cohort lost interest in headship over eighteen months is a striking, concrete data point illustrating the leadership pipeline crisis she describes.
Her line 'once the exceptional becomes routine, we have stopped describing commitment and started disguising bad design' sharply names how normalised over-sacrifice masks structural failure.
She cites Teaching Commission data (only 42% of deputies/assistant heads aspire to headship; average leader working 57.6 hours weekly) to ground her argument in current sector-wide evidence.

Her closing reframe - the better question is not 'how do we persuade people to want promotion?' but 'what do people see when they study the promoted?' - shifts responsibility from individual encouragement to system design.
quotes: I recently completed an NPQH. At the beginning of the course, almost all of the participants were interested in becoming a headteacher. By the end of the course, almost 18 months later, almost nobody was.

Only 42% of deputy and assistant heads say they aspire to headship, with workload, accountability and lack of support cited as reasons. Concern about work-life balance was the most common reason for avoiding promotion.
Once the exceptional becomes routine, we have stopped describing commitment and started disguising bad design.
Retention is not only about workload. It is about dignity. People stay where they can do good work without being made smaller by the system around them.
The better question is, What do people see when they study the promoted? If they see exhausted martyrs, they will opt out. If they see clever people reduced to inbox managers, they will opt out.
